old_title: Chancellor John Healey says banks are part of 'jewel in the crown' of UK economy, amid budget tax speculation - business live
new_title: Wall Street drops after jump in US producer inflation; John Healey says UK banks are part of 'jewel in the crown' - as it happened
old_text:
"I don't want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks' time.
My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.
That said, you know I've got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I'll set those out in two weeks' time.
Healey added that his "special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future" - echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago.
The chancellor also welcomed the IMF's support for the UK's fiscal plans.
US tech stocks are expected to fall when trading begins in under two and a half hour's time.
The futures market indicates the Nasdaq index could drop by around 1.2%, adding to yesterday's fall of almost 1.9%.
CharuChanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo says the markets are getting increasingly nervous, despite strong results from tech companies such as ASML and Micron, adding:
AI demand is not the problem; expectations and financing are. CoreWeave's bond selloff highlights growing scrutiny of debt-funded AI infrastructure and the cost of capital.
The IMF warned today that the Middle East region is suffering a highly uneven economic shock this year.
Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the Fund pointed out.
JihadAzour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told a news conference:
"The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries' ability to preserve macroeconomic stability."
Back in the financial markets, US government borrowing costs are heading for their biggest daily drop in over a year.
The sell-off in AI-linked stocks, such as chipmakers, today is driving investors into bonds instead. And the US, as well as the UK, is benefitting.
Ten-year US Treasury yields are down 11 basis points today to 5.08%, which Reuters has spotted would be the largest one-day decline since early August 2025.
Elsewhere in Bangkok today, Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden has said UK firms are trying to cut custs in response to the energy price shock, rather than just lift their prices.
That trend should make it easier for the central bank to contain inflation, and limit pressure to raise interest rates.
Speaking to CNBC TV on the sidelines of the IMF's annual meeting, Breedon said:
"What's really different now, relative to when we had the last energy shock in 2022, is that people aren't looking to push costs through.
"There's a desire to absorb the shock rather than just pass it on, which makes our job as monetary policymakers a bit easier in these uncertain times."
Healey: Banks are part of 'jewel in the crown' of UK economy
Intriguingly, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has told Bloomberg that banks are a part of the "jewel" in the UK's economic crown.
That, alongside his comments to UK journalists in Bangkok that banks are "hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects" could, perhaps, dampen speculation that the budget might contain a bank tax.
Last week, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) calculated that tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues.
The TUC argues that the government should reverse the cut to the bank surcharge made in 2023 by Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt.
Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year's budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk.
John Healey wrapped up his meeting with the UK press pack in Bangkok with a heavy hint that he is preparing to offer more support to Ukraine at the budget.
Healey, who was of course defence secretary earlier this year, said:
"Now is the time to step up pressure on Putin and step up support for Ukraine."
Asked if that could come as soon as the budget, Healey said:
"I'm working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine, military, diplomatic, and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it's what we see coming out of Ukraine, with Putin targeting these energy systems, leaving thousands without power, as we've got a harsh winter approaching.
The future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that's that's why it's so crucial that Putin doesn't prevail."
The press pack are now pressing John Healey on whether he will stick to the UK's fiscal rules (which were a big part of his predecessor Rachel Reeves).
Healey pledges to meet those rules (that day-to-day public spending must be covered by tax revenues, and that debt is falling as a share of GDP by the 2029/30 financial year).
Healey tells reporters in Bangkok:
"The test year is now just three years ahead, so this is a tighter set of fiscal rules than we had before. It's not five years out, four years out - it's in three years, 2029-2030, with borrowing set to fall and current spending covered by what we raise.
We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF's backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn't just a forecast for the future, but there's some evidence of performance already."
Asked about the potential economic benefits for the UK of potentially rejoining the European Union, JohnHealey said:
"Those sort of matters may become part of a wider conversation that the prime minister's keen to keen to encourage, because his basic starting point is one that very few people would dispute - that Brexit has not been good for for Britain.
But my task now, whatever happens in the future, is to make sure that we do our best to open up access to the markets where we can. That's what the European Summit is designed to do in specific areas. You know, we've got a big argument with Europe over the way that they frame their Made in Europe plans, just as we have over access to some of their defence.
And that big argument is, at this time of all times, when you have a strengthening US, a more resurgent China, actually, the strength of Europe beyond the European Union is enhanced in the economy and the national security side. If other European nations like us, like Norway, have contributions to make, we can do so with them."
Healey: won't engage in 'deeply damaging' pre-budget speculation
Heather Stewart
UK journalists then quizzed John Healey about specific tax options - including capital gains tax.
The chancellor responded that speculation ahead of previous budgets had been economically damaging.
Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok today, the chancellor says:
"Just in general terms, if you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging.
It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn't need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn't need to. So I'm just not going to get drawn into any speculation, especially as chancellor, especially this close to the budget."
Healey: Budget will give Britain a bit of breathing space
Heather Stewart
Asked about energy prices, JohnHealey then cited the government's VAT cut on electricity bills, saying:
"It doesn't remove the cost pressure. It recognises those pressures and says, look, where we can, we're a government that will act to try and give people a bit of breathing space. I've been very clear. Also, the prime minister's talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.
And then he tells journalists in Bangkok that the budget will give Britain "a bit of breathing space":
And so, I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space, but also reinforces the the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future."
"I don't want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks' time.
My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.
That said, you know I've got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I'll set those out in two weeks' time.
Healey added that his "special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future" - echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago.
The chancellor also welcomed the IMF's support for the UK's fiscal plans.
Healey: I will protect the resilience of the economy
UK chancellor John Healey has pledged to protect the 'resilience of the UK economy' when he presents his budget on 28 October.
Speaking to Sky News at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Healey said the IMF had backed Britain's plans this week, and upgraded its growth forecast for this year.
Speaking after the latest UK GDP report showed the economy kept growing, by 0.1%, in August, Healey say:
They [the IMF] say stay the path, and my budget will. It's my job, my responsibility as chancellor to make sure that I can protect that resilience in the British economy, and I will do that in the budget in two week's time.
The slump in tech stocks is helping to push down Britain's borrowing costs.
The yield, or interest rate, on UK debt has dropped today as investors buy up these gilts.
This has pushed the yield on UK 10-year bonds down by 10 basis points (0.1 of a percentage point) to 5.33% today.
Thirty-year gilt yields are down 10bps too, to 5.8%.
Neil Wilson, investor strategist at SaxoUK, explains what's occuring:
The sell-off across semiconductor stocks has sent bond yields lower, which if it sticks could ultimately support risk sentiment and support valuations.
This is two-fold; one a flight to relative safety with the risk-free rate generating 5%, and two, because a breakdown in the AI capex narrative and pullback in spend will shrink the supply of debt, the huge increase of which has been a powerful driver of bond yields moving out to multi-year highs.
Chip sell-off drags South Korea's Kospi index to six-month low
Oof! South Korea's benchmark Kospi share index has closed at a six-month low, as inflation fears and worries about the IT boom triggered a sell-off.
The Kospi ended the day down 7.5% at its lowest closing level since April, after a day of wild trading that briefly caused circuit breakers to be triggered. At its worst point, the Kospi was down over 9%.
Chipmakers drove the selloff - SamsungElectronics fell 9.5% and SKHynix plunged by 11.1%.
It's been a staggering year for South Korean traders. In the first half of 2026 the Kospi roughly doubled in value, as investors flocked to buy shares in chipmakers whose products were in hot demand with AI companies.
But that boom began to fade as we entered July. And now, the Kospi is 'only' up 30% for 2026.
The South Korean stock market boom was driven by a surge of interest from retail investors, many of whom bought shares on margin (with borrowed money), and could have lost their stakes as the market turned sour.
As covered earlier, today's tech rout is partly due to worries over US inflation, which may trigger interest rate rises.
There's also concern about the high amount of borrowing which AI firms are taking on as they roll out data centres and train new AI models.
LeeHardman of Japanese bank MUFG told clients this morning:
Bloomberg has reported that investor confidence in AI-related confidence has been undermined in part funding concerns.
CoreWeave, the world's biggest and most established neocloud, a relatively new term for companies that rent out computing power to AI model developers and teach leaders, saw its shares plunge in value by as much as 17% yesterday, and its debt due in 2032 traded at less than 78 cents on the dollar.
According to Bloomberg, credit default swaps on the company are pricing in more than a 50% chance of default within the next five years.
The London stock market is open, and shares in mining companies are dropping sharply.
Copper produder Antofagasta (-6.5%) is leading the fallers on the FTSE 100 share index, with RioTinto (-4.2%) and AngloAmerican (-4%) close behind. That may reflect concerns that a rise in US interest rates to fight inflation will dampen growth, and demand for commodities.
However, the wider FTSE 100 index is only down 0.1%. As it doesn't include many tech shares, it is insulated from the rout in chip stocks today. Instead, 'defensive shares' such as tobacco firms, consumer goods maker Haleon (+2.6%) and hotel chain Whitbread (+2.4%) are in demand.
Update: Antofagasta also released its latest production report this morning - this showed a 7% rise in third-quarter copper production, with the company maintaining its annual guidance.
Deutsche Bank: The UK's resilience story continues
The UK economy "surprised yet again" by growing by 0.1% in August, says Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank:
Raja explains that the UK's resilience story continues:
Undoubtedly, there may be some hiccups to come in the run up to year end, especially as energy prices continue to bite household incomes, and higher rates continue to drag on spending and investment.
The good news? The UK's resilience story continues. It's hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year. The UK economy remains the fastest growing G7 economy.
What's more impressive? If you believe the HMRC jobs data, UK GDP growth has hit 1.8% this year in the first eight months of the year, with 95k FEWER jobs. Who said productivity growth was dead in the UK?"

The US inflation squeeze has intensified, with new data showing that US producer prices rose in September at the fastest pace in more than four years.
With higher energy costs hitting the US economy, the producer price index advanced 1.3% from a month earlier - the most since March 2022. On an annual basis, prices were 6.3% higher.
The data helped to push down shares on Wall Street, as an accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets.
South Korea's benchmark Kospi 200index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.
US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers.
The UK rallied, though, helped by the news that Britain's economy kept growing.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.
With less than a fortnight before the budget, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.
John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight's time to offer consumers and businesses a "breathing space" while sticking to Labour's fiscal rules.
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.
My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects.
US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street's 'Epstein-connected' bosses to account
Kalyeena Makortoff
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street's "Epstein-connected" bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender's crimes.
It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for "dodging responsibility" over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.
A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.
If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate "Epstein connected" financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.
The UK stock market is continuing to benefit from turmoil elsewhere.
The FTSE 100 share index is now up 1.1% at 10,843 points, its highest level since 8 September.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says US assets are acting like a 'harbour in the storm':
A stronger economy, combined with a resilient FTSE 100, which is the best performing major index so far this week, is good news for the pound and the Gilt market. As other markets crash and burn, the pound is the top performing G7 currency this week, and the Gilt market is the best performer amongst its peers on Thursday. When the AI trade sells off, the UK is the harbour in the storm.
Coherent Corp, the US manufacturer of lasers, engineered materials, and optoelectronic components for AI data centres, is also caught up in the sell-off - its shares are down 9%.
Europe hasto take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.
Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy,said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were "targeted" and "temporary" so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.
Dell (-9%) are leading the fallers on the S&P 500, as doubts persist about the AI boom.
That adds to their 11% drop yesterday, after analysts at Barclays raised concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout.
Stocks are dropping on Wall Street at the start of trading, as inflation worries and AI angst hit share prices.
Tech stocks are leading the sell-off, pulling the Nasdaq index down by 1.3%.
The broader S&P 500 share index has dropped by 0.5%.
This morning's jump in the US PPI index will have raised concerns about inflationary pressures.
Traders are also reacting to the sell-off in Asia-Pacific markets overnight, where South Korea's Kospi hit a six-month low overnight (see earlier post).
On the AI front, AstraZeneca has entered into a new collaboration with a Californian AI therapeuticscompany called insitro, aimed at identifying novel targets to develop medicines for liver and heart disease.
The collaboration will focus on the areas of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a serious liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, diseases of the heart muscle.
Insitro has created a virtual human to generate large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design. The deal is worth $1.46bn, with $40m paid upfront by AstraZeneca. The Californian company also has partnerships with US drugmakers Bristol Myers-Squibb and Eli Lilly.
Sharon Barr, executive vice resident and head of biopharmaceuticals research & development at AstraZeneca, said:
"We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximising the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease.
Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster."
Today's jump in wholesale US inflation increases the pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.
WaleedSaid, technical analyst at GivTrade, says the increase in core PPI means the energy shock from the Iran war is spreading, adding:
A firmer Fed is more likely but the market pricing about a one in three chance of a hike in October so don't overreact to the headline but a rate hike in December does seem imminent.
New data from the US has shown that producers are hiking prices at their fastest rate in almost four years, and much faster than expected.
Ths increase was driven by a surge in energy prices, which more than wiped out a drop in egg prices.
The Producer Price Index, which measures how much goods makers and services firms charge for their wares, jumped by 6.3% in the year to September. That's the largest 12-month increase since December 2022, when it rose by 6.4%.
On a monthly basis, prices climbed by 1.2% in September alone, a sign that inflationary pressures rose last month.
The report shows that goods prices jumped by 2.6% in September alone, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.
That was driven by the rise in motor fuel; The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports:
Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent.
Alarmingly, core PPI also jumped. Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0% in the year to September.
PPI is an important measure, as increases in producer prices tend to be passed onto consumers, who already experienced a jump in inflation last month:
EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China
Jennifer Rankin
The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc's vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.
EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for "new instruments to better address these imbalances" according to a draft statement.
The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.
EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.
The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.
Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.
The EU's two biggest economies are also seeking "a diversification instrument" that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the "kill switch", the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.
Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise "they are killing their customers" , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.
The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU's point of view: "We don't have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost."
UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal
Media news: The UK government is 'minded to intervene' in Sky's£1.6bn deal to buy ITV's broadcasting and streaming arm.
Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, has told parliament she believes there are public interest grounds for intervening in the deal.
They include 'the need for free expression of opinion in news media', the need for a pluratity of views in the news, and the need for a wide range of broadcasting which is "of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests."
Back in July, Sky said the deal was a chance to create a "UK-focused national streaming champion".
